title: Verb-second (V2) word order
explanation: The finite verb is always the second element of a main clause, whatever occupies the first slot.
bridge_note: English does the same thing, just only after certain fronted words — "Never have I seen such a thing," "Only then did she realize." German just runs on this constantly instead of in a few fossilized cases.

title: Case marks articles and adjectives, not just pronouns
explanation: German has four cases (nominative, accusative, dative, genitive) marked throughout the sentence.
bridge_note: English mostly lost this except in pronouns (I/me, he/him, who/whom) — the concept isn't foreign, just far more limited in English.

title: Modal verbs push the infinitive to the end of the clause
explanation: The modal verb keeps second position, but the infinitive it governs parks at the very end, with anything else in between.
bridge_note: English keeps modal and infinitive stuck together ("have to work") — German is happy to separate them by a whole clause's worth.

title: Separable-prefix verbs split apart in main clauses
explanation: Verbs like aufstehen (to get up) split into the base verb and a stranded prefix at the end of the clause.
bridge_note: The closest English cousin is phrasal verbs behaving similarly ("I put my coat on"), though German is much stricter about exactly where the prefix lands.

title: Grammatical gender doesn't map onto English (or Portuguese) at all
explanation: der/die/das is a genuinely arbitrary system with no reliable shortcut from either language.
example_native: der Tisch, die Tür, das Buch
example_gloss: the table, the door, the book
bridge_note: Worth stating plainly rather than forcing a false bridge — this is the one point that's just memorization.

title: Plural formation is irregular and has to be memorized per noun
explanation: There's no single plural rule — nouns pluralize with an umlaut, an ending (-e, -er, -n, -s), both, or neither, and which one applies isn't predictable from the singular alone.
example_native: das Buch → die Bücher / das Auto → die Autos
example_gloss: the book → the books / the car → the cars
bridge_note: English mostly just adds -s and calls it done, with a small memorized set of exceptions (child/children, mouse/mice). German flips that ratio — the exceptions are the rule, and every new noun's plural has to be learned alongside its gender.

title: Everyday past tense is built with haben/sein + past participle
explanation: Spoken German mostly uses the Perfekt tense — a helper verb (haben or sein) plus the past participle — as its default past tense, even for plain, finished actions.
bridge_note: The shape matches English's present perfect ("I have eaten") exactly, but English reserves that for actions with present relevance, using simple past ("I ate") for a finished event. German uses the Perfekt for both — the familiar shape, doing more work than it does in English.

title: Adjectives before a noun take an ending that shifts with case, gender, and article
explanation: An adjective placed directly before a noun isn't left in its plain form — it takes an ending that changes depending on the noun's gender, case, and whether an article (and which kind) comes before it.
example_native: der gute Mann / ein guter Mann
example_gloss: the good man / a good man (same adjective, different ending)
bridge_note: English adjectives never change form no matter what they describe — this layer of agreement doesn't exist at all in English, so it's one of the purely additive rules with no shortcut, not just a different version of something already known.

title: In subordinate clauses, the verb moves to the very end
explanation: Clauses introduced by words like weil (because), dass (that), or wenn (if/when) push the finite verb all the way to the end of the clause, instead of keeping it in second position.
bridge_note: English keeps the verb right after its subject no matter what kind of clause it's in ("because I am sick" — verb stays put). German's main-clause V2 rule gets suspended entirely here, which trips up learners who've just gotten comfortable with verb-second.
